title: The example becomes your check value
idea: The output you worked by hand is exactly what you'll compare the real output to later. It is your check.

exercises.prompt: After coding, how do you use your hand-worked example?
options: Compare the real output to it
Throw it away
Rewrite it to match the code
Ignore it
exercises.explanation: The example is your check value. You run the code and compare what appears to what you expected.

exercises.prompt: If the real output matches your example, that's a good sign the code is right.
exercises.explanation: A match means the code did what you wanted. That's exactly why you wrote the example first.

exercises.prompt: Your example says the output is 'Hello'. The program prints 'Hello'. What now?
options: It matches — the task is done
Rewrite the example
It failed
Run it 10 more times to be safe
exercises.explanation: Real output matches the expected output, so the code passes this check. Nice work.

exercises.prompt: Your example says the output is 'Hello'. The program prints 'Hallo'. What now?
options: It does NOT match — fix the code
Change the example to Hallo
It's fine, close enough
The example was wrong
exercises.explanation: Hallo is not Hello. The example caught a real mistake. You fix the code, not the example.

exercises.prompt: If the output doesn't match, you should change your example to make it match.
exercises.explanation: Never bend the target to the result. The example is correct; the code is what needs fixing.

exercises.prompt: Put the full mini-rhythm in order.
blocks: Compare real output to the example
exercises.explanation: Example, then code, then check. The example you wrote first is the yardstick at the end.

exercises.prompt: Match each outcome to what it means.
exercises.explanation: A match passes, a mismatch means fix the code, and no example means no way to judge.

exercises.prompt: Which are good reasons the example is your 'check value'? (pick all)
options: It's the exact output you expect
You can compare it to the real output
It was decided before coding, so it's unbiased
It changes to match whatever the code does
exercises.explanation: Exact, comparable, and decided up front so it's honest. It must NOT change to match the code.

exercises.prompt: Task: 'show Red, then Blue'. Your example lists Red then Blue. The program shows Blue then Red. Pass or fail?
options: Fail — the lines are in the wrong order
Pass — both words appear
Pass — order never matters
Can't tell
exercises.explanation: Both words appear, but in the wrong order. Your example said Red first, so this is a fail — order is part of the check.

exercises.prompt: Writing the example first is what makes a later check possible.
exercises.explanation: No example, no check. The E step sets up the Check step — that's why we do it before coding.
